title: A Letter to God (poems: Dust of Snow, Fire and Ice)

topics.title: Faith of a farmer: reading and determiners

learn.hook: One hailstorm can flatten a whole field in ten minutes. What keeps a farmer going the next morning?
points: 'A Letter to God' is about a poor farmer whose crop is ruined by hail; his faith stays so strong that he writes a letter to God asking for help.
Literal questions are answered by words in the text; inference questions need clues, like a smile after a disaster showing hope.
Faith means complete trust; a person with faith expects help even when things look bad.
Determiners come before nouns: a, an, the, this, some, each, many, much, few, little.
Use many and few with countable nouns (many seeds, few clouds); use much and little with uncountable nouns (much water, little rain).

example.q: Passage: After the hailstorm, Hari's cotton field lay flat. His children cried, but Hari looked at the sky and smiled, 'Help will come.' Next morning he borrowed seeds and sowed again. What does Hari's smile tell us about him?
steps: His field is destroyed and his children are crying, so the situation is very bad.
Yet he smiles and says 'Help will come', so he is not giving up.
He also sows again the next day, which proves his hope is real.
example.answer: Hari has deep faith and hope; he trusts that help will come and acts on that trust.

learn.reallife: When a crop fails, many farmers in Maharashtra, Punjab or Odisha replant with seeds shared by neighbours. Faith and community help them start again.

games.title: Word and meaning
pairs: a storm of falling ice pellets

items.text: There were very ___ clouds in the sky in May.
___ farmers in the village came to help Hari.
Hari's wife made ___ cup of tea for every helper.
___ hailstones were as big as marbles.
We need ___ water to save these plants.

quiz.q: Passage: After the hailstorm, Hari's cotton field lay flat. His children cried, but Hari looked at the sky and smiled, 'Help will come.' Next morning he borrowed seeds and sowed again. What did Hari do the next morning?
options: He borrowed seeds and sowed again.
He sat and cried all day.
quiz.explain: The last line says he borrowed seeds and sowed again.
steps: The question asks about the next morning.
The last line says he borrowed seeds and sowed again.
Answer: He borrowed seeds and sowed again.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from general knowledge instead of reading the last line

quiz.q: Passage: After the hailstorm, Hari's cotton field lay flat. His children cried, but Hari looked at the sky and smiled, 'Help will come.' Next morning he borrowed seeds and sowed again. Which word best describes Hari?
quiz.explain: He smiles, says help will come and starts sowing again, so he is hopeful.
steps: Hari smiles, says 'Help will come' and sows again despite the loss.
These actions show he is hopeful, not greedy, lazy or angry.
Answer: Hopeful
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the children's feelings with Hari's

quiz.q: In 'A Letter to God', what ruins the farmer's crop?
quiz.explain: Rain first turns into a heavy hailstorm that destroys the crop.
steps: In the story, the rain the farmer welcomed turns into a heavy hailstorm.
The hail destroys the crop.
Answer: A hailstorm
quiz.mistake: Assumes the most common crop disaster instead of recalling the story

quiz.q: To whom does the farmer in 'A Letter to God' write his letter?
quiz.explain: His faith makes him write directly to God for money to sow again.
steps: The farmer's deep faith makes him ask God directly for money to sow again.
So he writes the letter to God.
Answer: God
quiz.mistake: Confuses the person who reads the letter with the one it is addressed to

quiz.q: What does the word 'faith' mean?
quiz.explain: Faith is complete trust or belief in someone or something.
steps: Faith means complete trust or belief in someone or something.
It is not fear or anger.
Answer: Complete trust
quiz.mistake: Links the word to the story's events instead of its meaning

quiz.q: Choose the determiner: 'We had ___ rain this monsoon, so the crops dried up.'
quiz.explain: Rain is uncountable, and 'little' means hardly any, which explains why crops dried up.
steps: 'Rain' is uncountable, so 'few' and 'many' (for countables) are wrong.
'Little' means hardly any, which explains why the crops dried up.
Answer: little
quiz.mistake: Uses few/many with an uncountable noun

quiz.q: Which sentence uses a determiner correctly?
options: He has much friends in the village.
He has a little friends in the village.
He has many friends in the village.
He has an friends in the village.
quiz.explain: 'Friends' is countable plural, so 'many' is correct.
steps: 'Friends' is a countable plural noun.
Countable plurals take 'many'; 'much' and 'a little' are for uncountables.
Answer: He has many friends in the village.
quiz.mistake: Uses much/little with a countable noun

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'hopeful'?
quiz.explain: Despairing means having lost all hope, the opposite of hopeful.
steps: Hopeful means expecting good things.
The opposite is despairing; cheerful, trusting and confident are close to hopeful.
Answer: Despairing
quiz.mistake: Picks a word with a similar, not opposite, meaning

teach.ask: Gappu: Why did the farmer keep trusting that help would come? And when do I say 'few' and when 'little'?
teach.praise: Chirp! Faith keeps hope alive, and few goes with things I can count. I get it!
teach.nudge: What kind of nouns go with 'few', and what kind go with 'little'?

revise.summary: 'A Letter to God' is about a poor farmer whose crop is ruined by hail, yet his faith makes him write to God for help. We also learn to answer literal and inference questions and to use determiners correctly.
focus: Recall story facts: a hailstorm ruins the crop and the farmer writes his letter to God.
Tell literal questions (answer is in the text) from inference questions (answer comes from clues).
Choose the right determiner for countable and uncountable nouns.
remember: Determiners come before nouns: a, an, the, this, some, each, many, much, few, little.
many/few + countable nouns (many seeds, few clouds); much/little + uncountable nouns (much water, little rain).
traps: Don't use few/many with an uncountable noun like rain: 'little rain', not 'few rain'.
Don't use much/little with a countable noun: 'many friends', not 'much friends'.
Don't answer from general knowledge; find the line in the passage.

learn.hook: A fire station catching fire. A traffic policeman getting a challan. Why do these make us smile?
points: Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what actually happens or is meant.
Verbal irony: saying the opposite of what you mean, e.g. 'Lovely weather!' during a storm. Sarcasm is a sharp form of verbal irony.
Situational irony: the result is the opposite of what was expected.
Dramatic irony: the audience or reader knows something a character does not.
In 'A Letter to God', the farmer calls the post office staff 'crooks', though they are the very people who collected money to help him.

example.q: Meena's brother laughed at her for carrying an umbrella on a sunny morning in Kochi. By noon, it poured, and he had to beg to share it. What kind of irony is this?
steps: The brother expected a dry day and thought the umbrella was silly.
The opposite happened: rain came, and he needed the umbrella himself.
An outcome opposite to what was expected is situational irony.

learn.reallife: Cartoons in newspapers and comedy shows often use irony, for example a 'No Honking' board on a road where everyone keeps honking.

games.title: Which kind of irony?
items: Stuck in a 3-hour jam, Kabir says, 'What a speedy ride!'
Looking at his burnt toast, Raju says, 'Perfect, just perfect.'
A swimming coach falls into the pool and needs rescuing.
A 'Save Paper' poster is printed on a thousand sheets of paper.
The audience knows the 'ghost' is the cook in a bedsheet, but the hero is terrified.
Readers know the gift box is empty, but the character thanks everyone loudly.

games.title: Irony check
items: Sarcasm is a form of verbal irony.
Sarcasm says the opposite of what is meant, usually to mock.
Dramatic irony happens when a character knows more than the audience.
It is the reverse: the audience knows more than the character.
A fire station catching fire is an example of situational irony.
We expect a fire station to stop fires, not suffer one.
Irony and simile mean the same thing.
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; irony is about a contrast with expectation.
In 'A Letter to God', the people the farmer calls 'crooks' had actually helped him.
The post office employees collected money for him, which makes his remark ironic.

quiz.q: What is situational irony?
options: When what happens is the opposite of what was expected
When a writer compares two things using 'like'
When a word imitates a sound
When the same sound starts several words
quiz.explain: Situational irony is a gap between the expected result and the actual result.
steps: Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what happens or is said.
Situational irony is when what happens is the opposite of what was expected.
Answer: When what happens is the opposite of what was expected
quiz.mistake: Confuses irony with other figures of speech

quiz.q: Stuck in a 3-hour traffic jam in Bengaluru, Kabir says, 'What a speedy ride!' What is this?
quiz.explain: Kabir says the opposite of what he means, which is verbal irony.
steps: A 3-hour jam is slow, yet Kabir calls it 'a speedy ride'.
Saying the opposite of what you mean is verbal irony.
Answer: Verbal irony
quiz.mistake: Thinks any ironic situation is situational irony, ignoring that he is speaking

quiz.q: In a school play, the audience knows the 'ghost' is just the cook in a bedsheet, but the hero shivers with fear. What is this?
quiz.explain: The audience knows something the character does not.
steps: The audience knows the 'ghost' is the cook; the hero does not.
When the audience knows more than a character, it is dramatic irony.
Answer: Dramatic irony
quiz.mistake: Focuses on the funny situation instead of who knows what

quiz.q: A swimming coach slips into the pool and has to be rescued by his students. Which kind of irony is this?
quiz.explain: We expect a coach to rescue others, but the opposite happens.
steps: We expect a coach to rescue swimmers, not be rescued.
The opposite of the expected result is situational irony.
Answer: Situational irony
quiz.mistake: Labels every humorous scene as verbal irony

quiz.q: In 'A Letter to God', why is it ironic that the farmer calls the post office employees 'a bunch of crooks'?
options: They were the ones who collected money to help him.
They had never read his letter.
They had refused to deliver his letter.
quiz.explain: The employees gave their own money; calling them crooks is the opposite of the truth.
steps: The post office employees gave their own money to help the farmer.
Calling his helpers 'crooks' is the opposite of the truth — that is the irony.
Answer: They were the ones who collected money to help him.
quiz.mistake: Takes the farmer's accusation as true

quiz.q: Which line shows verbal irony?
options: 'My phone died, so I asked a shopkeeper the way.'
'Oh great, my phone died just when I needed the map.'
'My phone is as dead as a stone.'
quiz.explain: 'Oh great' is said about a bad event, so the speaker means the opposite.
steps: Verbal irony says the opposite of what is meant.
'Oh great' about a phone dying at a bad time means 'how terrible'.
Answer: 'Oh great, my phone died just when I needed the map.'
quiz.mistake: Mistakes a simile or a plain statement for irony

quiz.q: Sarcasm is a sharp, mocking form of which kind of irony?
quiz.explain: Sarcasm is spoken, saying the opposite to mock, so it is verbal irony.
steps: Sarcasm is spoken mockery that says the opposite of what is meant.
So it is a form of verbal irony.
Answer: Verbal irony
quiz.mistake: Does not link sarcasm with spoken words

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a type of irony?
quiz.explain: Alliteration is the repetition of the same starting sound; it is a sound device, not irony.
steps: Verbal, situational and dramatic are types of irony.
Alliteration is a sound device (repeated first sounds), not irony.
Answer: Alliteration
quiz.mistake: Has not learnt the three types of irony

teach.ask: Gappu: My friend said 'Great job!' when I dropped the cake. Is that irony? What is irony, anyway?
teach.praise: Tweet! Irony is the opposite of what we expect or mean. My friend was being sarcastic!
teach.nudge: Is irony about what is expected versus what really happens or is meant? Can you name a type?

revise.summary: Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what actually happens or is meant. There are three types: verbal, situational and dramatic, and the farmer calling the helpful post office staff 'crooks' is ironic.
focus: Identify verbal, situational and dramatic irony in short examples.
Explain why it is ironic that the farmer calls the post office employees crooks.
Know that sarcasm is a sharp form of verbal irony.
remember: Verbal irony: saying the opposite of what you mean, e.g. 'Lovely weather!' during a storm.
Situational irony: the result is the opposite of what was expected.
Dramatic irony: the audience or reader knows something a character does not.
traps: Don't call every ironic scene situational irony; if someone says the opposite of what they mean, it is verbal irony.
Don't take the farmer's accusation as true; the employees collected money to help him.
Alliteration is not a type of irony; it is a sound device.

topics.title: Frost poems: symbols, mood and rhyme

learn.hook: Can a single bird change your whole day? Robert Frost thought so.
points: 'Dust of Snow' and 'Fire and Ice' are both by Robert Frost, an American poet.
In 'Dust of Snow', a tiny moment in nature (a crow shaking snow onto the poet) lifts his gloomy mood. The crow and hemlock, usually linked with gloom, bring a change for the better.
In 'Fire and Ice', fire stands for desire and ice stands for hatred; either could destroy the world.
A symbol is an object that stands for an idea beyond itself.
Rhyme scheme: give the same letter to lines whose last words rhyme (a, b, c ...).

example.q: Poem: A koel called from the neem tree, / Just when my sums went wrong; / My frown slipped off, I don't know how— / The day was saved by song. What is the rhyme scheme?
steps: Last words: tree, wrong, how, song.
tree = a, wrong = b, how = c (new sound), song rhymes with wrong = b.

learn.reallife: A cup of chai in the rain or a friend's joke can change a bad mood. Poets notice such small moments and turn them into poems.

games.title: Frost facts and poem tools
items: Robert Frost wrote both 'Dust of Snow' and 'Fire and Ice'.
Both poems in the lesson are by Robert Frost.
In 'Fire and Ice', ice stands for desire.
Ice stands for hatred; fire stands for desire.
A symbol is an object that stands for a bigger idea.
For example, a dove often stands for peace.
In 'Dust of Snow', a small event changes the poet's mood for the better.
The falling snow lifts his gloomy mood.
In a rhyme scheme, lines that rhyme get different letters.
Rhyming lines get the same letter.

quiz.q: Who wrote 'Dust of Snow' and 'Fire and Ice'?
quiz.explain: Both poems in the chapter are by Robert Frost.
steps: The chapter's two poems are 'Dust of Snow' and 'Fire and Ice'.
Both are by Robert Frost.
Answer: Robert Frost
quiz.mistake: Mixes up poets from other chapters of the book

quiz.q: In 'Fire and Ice', what do fire and ice stand for?
quiz.explain: Fire symbolises desire and ice symbolises hatred.
steps: In 'Fire and Ice', fire is linked to burning desire.
Ice is linked to cold hatred.
Answer: Fire: desire; ice: hatred
quiz.mistake: Reverses the two symbols or reads them literally

quiz.q: What is the central idea of 'Dust of Snow'?
options: A small moment in nature can change a bad mood
quiz.explain: A crow shaking snow onto the poet lifts his mood and saves his day.
steps: A crow shakes snow on the poet, and his gloomy mood lifts.
So a small moment in nature can change a bad mood.
Answer: A small moment in nature can change a bad mood
quiz.mistake: Reads the poem as a description of weather

quiz.q: Poem: A koel called from the neem tree, / Just when my sums went wrong; / My frown slipped off, I don't know how— / The day was saved by song. What is the rhyme scheme?
quiz.explain: Only lines 2 and 4 rhyme (wrong/song), so the scheme is abcb.
steps: Line-endings: tree (a), wrong (b), how (c), song (b).
Only lines 2 and 4 rhyme, so the scheme is abcb.
Answer: abcb
quiz.mistake: Assumes every line must rhyme

quiz.q: Poem: A koel called from the neem tree, / Just when my sums went wrong; / My frown slipped off, I don't know how— / The day was saved by song. What changed the speaker's mood?
quiz.explain: The koel called and the frown slipped off; the day was 'saved by song'.
steps: The koel called just when the sums went wrong, and the frown slipped off.
The day was 'saved by song' — the koel's call.
Answer: A koel's call
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sums were solved, which the poem never says

quiz.q: What is a symbol in poetry?
options: A word that sounds like its meaning
An object that stands for an idea beyond itself
quiz.explain: A symbol carries a deeper meaning, such as a dove for peace.
steps: A symbol is an object that stands for an idea beyond itself.
For example, a dove stands for peace.
Answer: An object that stands for an idea beyond itself
quiz.mistake: Confuses symbol with simile or rhyme

quiz.q: In 'Dust of Snow', the crow and the hemlock tree are usually linked with what?
quiz.explain: Both are commonly seen as signs of gloom, yet here they bring a happy change.
steps: The crow and the hemlock are usually seen as signs of gloom and sorrow.
Yet in the poem they bring a happy change.
Answer: Gloom and sorrow
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the contrast the poet creates

quiz.q: What does 'rue' mean?
quiz.explain: To rue something is to regret it.
steps: 'Rue' means to feel sorry about something.
So it means regret.
Answer: Regret
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the sound of the word

teach.ask: Gappu: How can snow or a bird change someone's mood? And what do fire and ice mean in Frost's poem?
teach.praise: Hoot-hoot! Small things can change a mood, and fire and ice are symbols of desire and hatred. Clever Frost!
teach.nudge: What do fire and ice each stand for in the poem?

revise.summary: Robert Frost's 'Dust of Snow' shows a small moment in nature lifting a gloomy mood, and 'Fire and Ice' uses fire for desire and ice for hatred. We also learn what a symbol is and how to work out a rhyme scheme.
focus: Know the central idea of both Frost poems.
Explain the symbols: fire = desire, ice = hatred; crow and hemlock usually linked with gloom.
Work out a rhyme scheme by giving the same letter to rhyming line endings.
remember: Both poems are by Robert Frost, an American poet.
A symbol is an object that stands for an idea beyond itself.
Rhyme scheme: give the same letter to lines whose last words rhyme (a, b, c ...).
traps: Don't reverse the symbols: fire is desire, ice is hatred.
Don't assume every line must rhyme; tree/wrong/how/song gives abcb.
'Dust of Snow' is not just a weather poem; it is about a change of mood.
